utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, you will have the accused brought in, please? (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters, those who transmit, transfer, translate our words. We will pick up where we stopped after I have asked the registrar to be kind enough to bring in Brigadier Zeko. Mr. Nobilo, a brigadier, that's a general of the brigade, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm not a military expert, but this is the rank following the rank of colonel in the Croatian army. Therefore, in some armies, it is considered to be brigadier general, and in other armies, the rank is called brigadier, but it is the rank above colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Nobilo, a question. What is a colonel general?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A colonel general is a much higher rank than the brigadier, because we have major general, colonel general, and general of the army, a five-star general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Zeko, General Zeko, Brigadier General Zeko, please be seated. We're going to resume where we broke off with your cross-examination. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have nothing to hide from you. I was just asking the correspondence of your rank of brigadier. You're a General, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, if we call you "General," you won't mind. On the contrary, I hope.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is my future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, General. We can now continue with the re-examination where we stopped. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I won't take long, and I shall try to finish this off within a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Re-examined by Mr. Nobilo:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, while you were working in Slovenia in the JNA, you were working in the same area as Tihomir Blaskic. Were you privately friends, acquaintances?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, your education. You completed the academy, but, as far as I know, you also had speciality training as an intelligence officer following the academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it also true that you are the only educated intelligence officer, one with specialist training in 1993, not only in Central Bosnia, but in the HVO as a whole?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has asked you about reconnoitring, and you used two terms; once you said a unit, then you said a group. Can you tell us how many people go to reconnoitre behind enemy territory, enemy lines?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, three to five men go on reconnaissance missions, and during this reconnoitring, they should use concealed approaches, those concealed from the enemy, and they usually use inaccessible terrain where the enemy least expects anyone to come from, concealed from the enemy. This infiltration into enemy territory takes a lot of time, depending on the assignment given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you use various types of camouflage that we know from films, like branches and twigs and crawling along the ground?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes. All types of camouflage are used, adjusted to the season. If not clothing, then you use other devices to be found in the terrain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that dangerous? Have there been any deaths and woundings?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes. There were people who were wounded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go on to the questions of the Prosecutor regarding communications, telephone and fax use. Your command was in Bila. The Operative Zone had its command in the Vitez Hotel. Between you in Bila and the Vitez Hotel, was there an underground telephone cable?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that telephone link go through territory under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the telephone exchange, was it in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that, within the Vitez-Busovaca enclave, there was a reliable telephone link and a telefax which the enemy could not intercept?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, you had no problems with regard to telephone communications with the command?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the situation like with regard to Kiseljak? Where did the underground telephone links go from Vitez-Busovaca to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Those underground cables went via Busovaca-Kiseljak and between Kacuni and Bilalovac to Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From January 1993, who controlled the area between Kacuni and Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: It was under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be right to say that the telephone lines passed through territory which was under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, what about this telephone line to Kiseljak, passing through territory under BH army control, was it safe from interception and the tapping of faxes?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. It was not safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you observe that and did that prompt you to stop using it? If so, when?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes. We noticed this already in March of 1993, that there were disturbances which prompted us to believe that our messages were being tapped and intercepted, those being conveyed along that route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, I think there were five lines, and all of them were operational. After that, at least four broke off, and one was being intercepted. When the war started in April, would any commander, in your opinion, decide to use that line going through enemy territory to convey precise information about the deployment of its units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Because he would be disclosing the position of units, the deployment of units, and the activities being undertaken by those units, which, of course, would be to the benefit of the enemy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that inexperienced HVO soldiers frequently used hand-held radio transmitters, speaking over those phones, after which, this would be followed by the heavy shelling of units?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the technology of a modem and packet links. Could you explain to the Court, this computer technology that you used, those software programmes, were they specialised military programmes or regular computer programmes that you can buy in any civilian store selling computers?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Those are civilian programmes that were commercially available, and those are the ones we used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I understood was that modem links and packet links are more or less the same. I don't know anything about computers, so please correct me if I'm wrong. You would write a text, you would store it in a file, and to open the file, you would determine a certain number or a group of numbers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't encrypt the text?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Therefore, if anyone wanted to intercept your telephone conversations or from the air, all he needed to do was to have the password to enter the file and to read everything that you were sending?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't that being done nowadays by 14-year-olds who are finding it very simple to discover those passwords?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is nothing specially designed for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. Mr. Nobilo is testifying, and he is asking only for a "yes" or a "no" answer. I think it would be more appropriate to have the witness asked the questions and explain, in his own words, the answers to these particular questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I know you're doing military training in the area of communications, but that is not the purpose of this hearing. Please, put your questions, avoid comments, and then tonight you can see what was being said regarding military matters. Please pose your questions directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. I was only trying to save time, and I learned about this method of questioning in this courtroom. It is not permitted in my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please don't do something that you seem to be doing on purpose. That's what you're telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It's only for the sake of expediency, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were there in your intelligence department for the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Only eight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that, apart from you, there were two more officers. Were they officers with military academy training?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. They did not graduate from the military academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was your office dislocated to Bila in relation to the command?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Primarily because of space considerations, because in the Vitez Hotel, there wasn't enough room, and also for safety reasons. We didn't want to have the whole command in one place, because shelling was quite frequent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you whether you worked with officers from the Croatian army. You said no. He asked you whether there were Croatian army troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You said no. My question is: During the Croat and Muslim war in 1992/1993, which is the period covered by this indictment, did you see Croatian army troops or a Croatian soldier in that period?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go outside the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia in that period?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I did not in that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that you didn't see any Croatian soldiers, you mean you didn't see them in Central Bosnia, because you didn't go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone wear uniforms with "HV" insignia in the Busovaca-Vitez enclave?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: These insignia were worn by soldiers who were living in Central Bosnia but who, during the war in Croatia in 1991, went to the battlefront at the beginning of the war in Bosnia. They returned to their homes where they joined the struggle, and they didn't take off those HV insignia, wishing to prove, thereby, that they were superior to the locals and that they had some wartime experience, more experience than people who had not been on the front until then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this applied to a limited number of individuals only?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, only individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In a document yesterday, there was mention of 2.300 soldiers from Mehurici, 160 were engaged on the front against the Serbs. Can you tell the Court, because that is what the Prosecutor asked you on several occasions, on a day when the front with the Serbs was not moving, and it wasn't in 1993, how many BH army soldiers, in all, were engaged on the front against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: At that time, at these frontlines that were not moving, a total of 1.000 to 1.500 soldiers of the BH army were engaged on the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question has to do with the Prosecutor's question about the shelling of Zenica from Serb positions. Tell the Court, according to the sources of the BH army, as well, was there repeated shelling of Zenica from Serb positions?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next question is linked to the order of Colonel Blaskic of the 17th of April, mentioned by the Prosecutor and which you had not seen. Linked to that order, I'm asking you the following: Immediately prior to the April war between the Croats and Muslims, where were the most significant forces of the BH army concentrated in Kiseljak municipality, including their command, military police, and so on?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: They were concentrated in the area of Gomionica, Svinjarevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Next, Prosecution Exhibit 472, can it be shown to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document which the Prosecution showed you, and it has to do with a report by Franjo Nakic, Chief of Staff of the Headquarters, addressed to Colonel Blaskic in Kiseljak on the 30th of January, 1993. When you were shown this report, which you confirmed the authenticity of and the signature of Franjo Nakic, can you, indeed, confirm that he was in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court how come you didn't know that Blaskic was in Kiseljak and not in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: At first, when I introduced myself, I said I was assistant chief of staff for intelligence affairs and that my superior was the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that you were in contact on a daily basis with the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From this document, document 472, it emanates that you were at the meeting on the 27th of January '93 with Mr. Flemming, and that Mr. Flemming said, among other things, and I quote, these are the last four lines of this text regarding Lasva and Dusina, he says, "... that it was hard to avoid the feeling that something terrible had happened." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Court what is the terrible thing that happened in Lasva and Dusina, as far as you remember?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: The villages of Lasva and Dusina were the first targets of attack by the BH army carried out by the Lasva operative group under the command of Nehru Ganic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this. This is beyond the scope of the examination. The fact that it's mentioned in an exhibit, and there are no questions about that, Mr. President, does not invite thorough examination of what happened in Lasva and Dusina, without the ability of the Prosecutor, in my view, to come back and ask questions about what is newly tendered evidence. The document speaks for itself. The testimony of Brigadier Zeko is new on this particular subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is true, that we are going outside, considerably, the scope of the questions put during the cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo, what was the meaning of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The meaning of the question was an explanation of these words which appear in the document that were shown to our witness yesterday, and that is that Mr. Flemming said that something terrible had happened in Lasva and Dusina. So my question is a clarification, what does this word "terrible" mean, because it is all a relative issue. If the Court feels that we should go on, we would be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But now that the question has been rephrased, will you please briefly answer what the word "terrible" implies?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: It means that the BH army captured those villages and expelled the inhabitants of those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any killing of civilians?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we go on to the next question now? You told the Prosecutor that the BH army was well-equipped. When you say "well-equipped," could you clarify this? This is a relative concept. Does it mean "well" compared to modern armies, such as the NATO army, or in relation to the Serbs, or in relation to the Croats? What does a well-equipped BH army in April '93 mean for you?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: "Well-equipped" means as compared to the HVO, and poorly equipped compared to the Bosnian Serb army and NATO standards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the greatest shortage in the equipment of the BH army clothing and footwear?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, did the HVO, on any occasion, voluntarily abandon the front against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No, it did not, until the BH army carried out an attack from behind in the region of Travnik and Novi Travnik against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now can I call for the usher's assistance with the document, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is D197, 197A the French translation, 197B in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the last document and the last question that we are going to have, Mr. President. I feel obliged to explain something to you personally. When the witnesses from Ahmici were here at some point, you warned me against some questions which you considered not to be relevant, and I answered that three months later I will be able to explain that to you. Unfortunately not three, but nine months have elapsed since, but I will be able to explain everything today. This is a diary found in Ahmici, and it obviously belongs to somebody from Ahmici. One day we call a witness who found that diary. Here there is a plan with all the positions, all the names of the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Nobilo. Just before you continue with your cross-examination, I suppose that the document that you are distributing is within the scope of this cross-examination. You know that during re-examination you can bring new documents, this is your right; but I just want to know that this is within the scope of the cross-examination. I don't know anything of it, but I'm asking you the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would request that we have the opportunity to inspect this document and also have the opportunity to ask any questions about it that have been raised in the redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, you're going to ask questions -- only we see that this document is outside of the scope of the cross-examination. In that case, the Judges will refuse, and that is why I made this caution to Mr. Nobilo. He told to us Judges that he was sure of his position. And now, Mr. Harmon, if this document is interesting to the Judges, but if it, nevertheless, is outside of the scope of the cross-examination, we will give you the right to reply. But for the time being, we are not there, yet, and Mr. Nobilo is now using his right to distribute documents. According to the good principles, it is better to be safe than sorry. I thought it was better to warn you against it beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, we always should be cautious, that is why I made this introduction. We are offering as evidence only what was written on the 11th of April, 1993, and it concerns a telegram that arrived and that said that the units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina should be put in a state of readiness, and that was five days before the beginning of the conflict. The witness was telling us about the intentions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to attack the Lasva Valley, and putting the units into combat readiness is the last stage. So, what was written on the 11th of April, that is the only thing that we want to tender as evidence from this diary. Later on, we will come back and use this diary, as well. As you can see, here it says "Sunday, the 11th of April, 1993," that was five days before the war broke out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the moment we are not concerned with the totality of this document, Mr. Prosecutor, but only with the six or seven lines, at least, that is the case in the French version. For those of you who follow the French version, this is on page 6. Mr. Nobilo, please, now present this part of your document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let's make this thing clear. You have never seen this journal, this diary before?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will read the entry for the 11th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, if this witness has never seen this document before he is not the appropriate witness to introduce this document. Furthermore this document has never been authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But he knows the contents of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Harmon, let Mr. Nobilo finish, and I suppose he will see whether this witness can or cannot identify this document. This is a rule that we have adopted here with my colleagues, Judge Riad and Judge Shahabuddeen. In general, when one or the other party makes an objection, we should at least let the other party present its point of view first. First, Mr. Nobilo, and after that, Mr. Harmon. If you want you can still make your objection, but later on. Now, Mr. Nobilo, you can talk to your witness concerning those six lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me now read the six lines, and now you will answer to me whether you know of this event, what you know of the circumstances which caused that event, and what you know of that event, or if you don't know. "The 11th of April, 1993, Sunday, at five o'clock, a meeting was held at the school Zumara. The agreement was made where the lines will be formed in case there will be any shooting. I kept the watch between 10 and 12, and around 11 o'clock I heard that a telegram had arrived." And then the quotation about putting of the units in the first stage of combat readiness. And the rest is not relevant. Now, I'm asking you: Do you know about telegrams of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina which, on that day, were forwarded to the units telling them to prepare for the first stage of combat readiness? Were you aware of that in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain that. On the 10th of April we received a telegram of the corps command about an organisational command for all units, and this is a telegram sent to one of the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, what you want to say, is that you used technical measures like tapping?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, we received a telegram through -- it is an organisational command that was sent to all units, and we decrypted it, and then we followed the situation on the ground with the units that observed and followed and monitored the movements of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is all that I had to ask about this particular document, and this has been my last question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you like to make an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I would make an objection to the admissibility of this document, Mr. President. It has not been authenticated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, can you give us some elements that could help this witness to identify this document? Because it is true that this document -- well, the Prosecutor is going to have inconveniences if he is later going to reply. We cannot know where these pages come from. Can you say that or you cannot say that for the moment, and in that case we can postpone its admissibility for the moment. What would you prefer?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, another witness will authenticate this document. At this moment we wanted just to authenticate the six lines written on the 11th of April. At this stage we are not asking to authenticate this Serb document through this witness. We can postpone it to the moment when the witness will come here, the witness who had actually found this diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As the Defence does not, in particular, wish this document to be admitted, this document has not been admitted into evidence for the moment, so, we will not give it a number. But it will probably be authenticated through another witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, this document has already been marked for identification, but it has not been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you, I believe everybody is agreeable on that. So, I think that we have finished now with all the questions by the Defence, by the Prosecution, and by the Defence, and now I'm turning to my colleagues. Judge Riad, do you have any questions you would like to ask? Please do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier Zeko.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to clarify some general points, and I hope that the knowledge that you have and you've given us, proof up to now, you will be able to clarify these points. What interests me is whether the army of Territorial Defence, the army that had existed before the HVO was formed, were the members of that army, were the members both Croatian and Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, before the conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, there was an army that was a joint army. There was the Territorial Defence and the HVO. And at the beginning the TO had both Croatian and Muslim members. I, myself, was one of the members of that army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And later, they split up. You said that the BH army had something between 80.000 to 82.000 soldiers and the HVO had 8.000 soldiers. How can you explain this difference? Was it that the soldiers that were in the initial army were mostly Muslim? If they both belonged to the same army, they should have been more or less in the same proportions and not such a huge number of Muslims and such a small number of Croats.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we spoke about the territory of Central Bosnia, and what I was speaking of is that apart from the existing population of the Central Bosnia. The greatest part of the refugees that came from the Krajina region and from other regions with Muslim majority, they were coming to Central Bosnia. And that is why the proportions have such a big difference; whereas the Croats that had been expelled by the Bosnian Serb army, they mostly left for Croatia. For example, from the Krajina region, all of them, they went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes, but even the soldiers had gone? Were there only 8.000 soldiers left? All the others, the soldiers had gone to Croatia. How come there was only 8.000 Croatian soldiers? The only explanation that you gave was that Central Bosnia had a Muslim majority. Is that the explanation?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Not only that, but, as I've said, from those areas under the control of Bosnian Serbs, the refugees from those areas were coming to Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And they belonged to the army?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Not all of them were in the army. The displaced persons were also civilians and children. But apart from the Bosnian Krajina and all the eastern part, Eastern from Doboj, everything, there was a great flow of refugees into the Central Bosnian region, which was not under the control of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In that Bosnian army were there Mujehadeen? You told us the Mujehadeen came from Afghanistan and Iran.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And how come? What caused the Mujehadeen to come there? Why were they made to come to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: The real reason I could not explain to you now, but they used as an excuse to provide help to the Muslim brothers. That was the slogan of those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who made them come? Was it the state, or did they just come to the country, or did the government call them so that they would help with the defence?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Had the government asked them to help, I don't know. I cannot give you an exact answer. But they did not come all at the same time. They used to come gradually through various humanitarian organisations that, at the time, were arriving in the Central Bosnian region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You call these humanitarian organisations. What do you mean by that? Did the humanitarian organisations bring combatants?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No, they did not organise the combatants' arrivals, but that is the way, that is how they would mostly be arriving. That is what my colleagues were telling me, that they would go across Croatia and then come to Bosnia. Those Mujehadeen, those that called themselves Mujehadeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: According to the report by Colonel Blaskic, and I even notice here the translation, the Bosnian army was poorly equipped. What you said was that, on the contrary, that army was well-equipped. How come that army was so well-equipped when their sanctions, there was an arms embargo on the whole of Yugoslavia; so how come that army would be so well-equipped? One that interests me, first of all, is the Bosnian army, BH army.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, when I said "well-equipped," what I had in mind was well-equipped from the point of view of weapons, and compared to the HVO. When it comes to comparison with the army of Bosnian Serbs, that army was poorly equipped; but BH army did not pay great attention to the clothing of the soldiers. So, they paid more attention to armaments and ammunition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Where did those weapons come from?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer as to where the weapons came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Through Croatia or through Serbia, or through where?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, it's a rare day that the Defence will interrupt any of your question, but we need the witness's passport. His visa expires today and I believe he has his passport with him. We need to extend it through tomorrow so he will be able to go home and return to his duties. May I ask the witness if he has his passport to give it to me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: When I have finished he can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Obviously we are not going to try and keep Brigadier as hostage at this Tribunal. So, please, can you assist Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We need your passport, Mr. Zeko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and again, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would like to -- I thought for a moment that the witness had to go. I would like to continue with my questions. You are a member of the intelligence service, and I suppose that you knew what was going on. How come the BH army, for which you claim it was well-equipped, where did they get the weapons from? And later on I will ask you the same question for the HVO. I will not ask for the Serb army because you're not a specialist on that.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: The supply of arms during the war depended on how one could manage. Partly it was taking the armaments and equipment from the former JNA that was on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that armament had remained there. There were other channels and I think the only way was through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Croatia provided equipment for the BH army?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't know whether Croatia armed them, but I know that they both, the Muslims and the Croats, could receive any armament via Croatia. But I cannot say that it was Croatia who supplied that armament and that equipment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen is going to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Brigadier, I am one of those slow speakers. I hope that does not trouble you too much. Let me ask you the first question like this. You were talking about October, 1992. You were mentioning a roadblock, which I thought you said the BiH put up to stop HVO forces from going to Jajce to fight the Serbs. You were saying that the HVO was going to Jajce to fight the Serbs, but I understood you to say that the BiH put up a roadblock to stop them. Is my recollection correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the first incident that happened and that you mentioned was the putting up of roadblocks by the then Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. At that time the army had not been formed as yet. There were the HVO units that were going for a tour of duty in Jajce where the frontlines were of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do I understand you to mean that the territorial units were the predecessors of the BiH?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So, there were Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, tell me this; why would Muslim forces stop the HVO from going ahead to fight the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the reason why I cannot explain, but I know that at that time we still worked together, and that after that incident an agreement was reached. There was a meeting, and then two or three days later those soldiers managed to get through to Jajce. But why it happened at that time, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Tell me about the Mujehadeen. Were they present during the period when the relations between the HVO and the Muslim forces were good or did they arrive afterwards? That is to say, did they arrive after relations had soured?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: The arrival of the Mujehadeen in the region of Central Bosnia happened in mid 1992, but at that time, they were still working illegally in a clandestine way, and they would mostly go to villages. The first destination in Central Bosnia was the village of Mehurici, which means that when it came to the escalation or, we can say, when the conflict broke out between the HVO and the BiH army, at that moment, quite openly, the Mujehadeen units started to participate. There were units such as Abdul Latif and El Mujahed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What do you say about this: Did the HVO receive any reinforcements by way of personnel from any of the former republics of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, and in the time period when I was there in that region, that is, the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, I have no knowledge of it. I do not know that any units arrived from other republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you be so kind as to answer the same question in relation to the BiH? Did they receive reinforcements in the form of personnel from any of the former republics of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, can you describe the relations between the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Croats in this sense: Was there any period during which the Serb military forces were in a state of cooperation with the Croat military forces?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: In that period, whether there was any cooperation, I know, personally, nothing of, because in the Lasva River Valley where I was, in that enclave of the Lasva Valley, there was certainly no cooperation. As for other enclaves that were separate from ours, I cannot claim anything, because I was not there at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, as my colleague, Judge Riad, has had occasion to observe, you drew a comparison between the size of HVO military forces and the size of BiH military forces, and I think the ratio you gave was roughly 10:1 as against the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Can you also describe matters in such a way as to present the picture of the HVO being contained in two relatively small geographical pockets and surrounded on all the sides by BiH forces. Was that the picture you presented?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, tell me about this: You were an intelligence officer, and you were concerned with evaluating the strength and the positions of the opposing forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, could you meaningfully evaluate the strength of the opposing forces without, at every stage, making comparisons with the strength of the forces on your side?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, it is quite obvious that a comparison cannot be made if we do not know how many forces, what was the personnel strength on the other side. Otherwise, you can't establish a proportion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you make a schematic of the HVO forces and of their distribution?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No. The total amount is given by the command or by the operatives. They are the ones who give the full personnel strength.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, with this huge advantage of forces, how do you explain the fact, I believe it is a fact, that the BiH did not succeed in overwhelming the HVO and in taking over these two relatively small pockets?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, apart from those two pockets existed another three pockets, because there were five enclaves under the command of the Operational Zone of Central Bosnia. We were speaking of the Lasva River Valley, where you've noticed there were two pockets which are relevant for this particular case. How can we say that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina could not take control? It did in quite a great deal, because this enclave was split up into five parts. And could the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it probably could have taken control over the whole region, had a peace agreement not been reached. So we cannot claim that the BH army was not able to win control over it, but I think what is crucial is to know the time period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: We're talking about April 1993, more or less. What proportion of the BiH strength, would you say, was directed to the Serbs and to the other HVO pockets to which you have referred?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Talking about the balance of forces in the time period that we are referring to, it was not possible to establish precisely the balance of forces, because there were people on a daily basis. For example, an entire brigade would come from Jajce to the Central Bosnia area, which immediately changes the balance. At the time of the conflict between the HVO and the BiH army, the ratio of forces was the one that I presented in my estimate. Sometimes it may have been lower, and, according to some estimates, their number went up to 97.000, occasionally. But while the conflicts were ongoing between the HVO and the BiH army, the frontlines towards the Serbs were not moving, and so I already gave you this ratio of forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If the frontlines towards the Serbs were not moving, would I be right in supposing that the frontlines were not moving because they were opposed by the BiH?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Are you referring to the front-line between the Bosnian Serb army and the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, because on those frontlines in that time period, the front-line did not move between the Bosnian Serb army and the lines held by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I know, Brigadier. I know that you have said that the frontlines did not move. I'm asking you this question: Is it the case that the frontlines did not move because the BiH was opposing the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I would say that, in this period, that was not so, because the BH army had established contact with the Bosnian Serb army in the area of Meokrnje and in the area of Turbe, and I'm referring to the enclave of the Lasva Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: If the BiH had not established contact with the Serbs, as you said, would the Serbs have been in a position to advance even further?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: This is a question that I don't know how to answer. I don't know whether the Serbs would have started an offensive. In my personal opinion, the Serbs, in this time period, did not, themselves, want to join in, probably waiting for the outcome of the conflict between these two belligerents, the HVO and the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put my last question on this phase to you: Was any part of the total BiH forces, amounting to some 82.000 people, directed to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you like to say, since you have been dealing with estimates, what portion of the 82.000 men, Muslim BiH men, would have been concentrating on the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: On the defence lines, I have already said there were between 1.000 and 1.500 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. What part of the 82.000 men would have been concentrating on the other HVO pockets to which you have referred?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: In military terminology, this is a ratio of 1:10, as we have already said. However, these 84.000 were not all, at the same time, waging war. These are units that the BiH army had at its disposal within the territory of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. They were the units of the 3rd Corps, the entire 3rd Corps, parts of the 1st Corps, parts of the 2nd Corps, and parts of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let's turn to the business of resupply. Is my impression correct that you have said that the BiH got their resupplies through territory held by the HVO? If I'm wrong, do correct me.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would that mean, then, that the HVO was in a position to control the extent of military supplies reaching the BiH?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that. I don't know. Whatever I were to give could not be authentic, because I was not in a position to be able to see whether it could control it or not. But the fact is that the supplies went through territories under the control, among others, of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me put the question a little hypothetically to you. If the HVO was in a position to control the extent of military resupplies to the BiH, was it, in your judgement, likely that the HVO would permit the BiH to be better equipped than the HVO itself?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Logic tells us that no one would allow it, but I'm talking about the period of the conflict, not while we're operating together.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you made certain estimates and assessments for the HVO, and I take it that your assessments and estimates were made on an objective basis; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: My estimates were made on the basis of information gathered in the ways I have presented and on the basis of the situation on the ground during this war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I mean is, the estimates you presented to the HVO authorities would enable the HVO to decide, on the basis of those estimates, whether they wanted to attack or to defend?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: The estimates made were certainly used to take steps in relation to the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I'll put it slightly differently. Your estimates would not vary, depending on whether the objective of the HVO authorities was offensive or defensive. Estimates would remain the same. Somebody else would decide whether, on the basis of your estimates, they wanted to take offensive action or defensive action?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I'm a little unclear. Your evidence was quite extensive. I have a problem with pronunciation, and this could mislead you. I remember some talk about Gomionica, does that ring a bell for you, and of an attack being ordered by General Blaskic on the 17th of April, 1993. Do you recall that area of testimony? I think you said you didn't remember it yourself.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: At that time, I did not because I said that I did not have information from Kiseljak at that time. But according to information I had before, units of the BiH army were situated in the area between Gomionica and Svinjarevo, with their command post in Gomionica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What about Stara Bila, was there an HVO attack there in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: In Stara Bila, an active defence was carried out, and this was at the feature known as Grbavica, to prevent the breakthrough of the BiH army towards the explosives factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You are not aware of any attacks mounted by the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, to carry out an attack, there must be a certain depth, which means moving the defence by about 800 metres. In military terms, this is described as an active defence, because there wasn't any operation in strategic or operative terms. This was strategic movement of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What is the standard military wisdom about the proportionalities involved in mounting an attack? The attackers must have a certain ratio of advantage. What is that, 3:1, 2:1?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: In the army I was serving, it was 2:1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So if a party mounted an attack, we could suppose that that party had a 2:1 advantage or thought it had a 2:1 advantage?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in this case, in this war, the principles that we referred to were not respected. I'm talking about the principles that were started at the academy at which I studied. In this case, the ratio could have been much higher or much lower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Things were unorthodox?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a little about some documentation. I begin with Exhibit 195. It is dated, let me see, it begins during the day, the Mujehadeen. I wonder whether you have seen it. I would ask the registrar to show it to you, in case you haven't seen it recently. It speaks of the Mujehadeen. Did you receive a copy of this document at the time?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When did you go into the area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: At the time it was issued, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: When did you go into the area? When did you assume command of your particular post?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: This is a document that refers to a period much earlier, but I had it in my files. It was in the archives of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The document is dated the 22nd of April, 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: This is a mistake. I think it should be '93.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Does "1992" appear in the original?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And the month is April, the 22nd of April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question like this: Have you experienced a certain risk that early in the year, say, January, you tend to carry over the previous year and write that year in, instead of writing in the new year? If you pass from 1991 to 1992, in January, you still tend to write, now and then, the previous year. Have you experienced that?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No? Do you think that well into the year, in April of a given year, you would write in the previous year for the current year?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Let us understand one another. This is not a document drafted by me or my department. It was sent to me by the assistant for intelligence from the Viteska Brigade. This text, the contents, refers to 1993. It may have been an error, a typewriting error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand. I retract any suggestion that you, yourself, might have written it. I was only speaking rhetorically. I understand very fully that your testimony is that you didn't write this, you only received this. Let me rephrase the question by asking: Does your experience suggest to you that the writer of a memorandum who is writing in April of a year would write in the previous year for the current year, he might do that in January and maybe early February, and do you think he would do that in April?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Whether he may have done it, according to what I see, the mistake was made. Whether it could have been done, I -- the year has been typed erroneously. Instead of "1992," we have "1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Brigadier, if we could turn to 194, it's a document dated the 16th of April. The Prosecutor read out some parts of paragraph 1 to you. Roughly, in paragraph 1, the BiH was saying that the HVO were committing brutal aggression. Was that correct or not correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: As far as I know, and judging by the activities I engaged in, for me, this is not correct, that the HVO was carrying out a brutal aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So, you recognise that, according to your assessment of the document, there could be a problem of determining what parts are correct and what parts are not correct?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: In this document, and the sentence that you quoted, I just expressed my personal opinion regarding this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you turn to paragraph 4 and help me? Not being a military man, I cannot interpret all the formulations correctly. I see that this paragraph speaks of an attack; does any particular part of it speak directly or indirectly of a BiH attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: No mention is made of the attack on Ahmici. The only thing mentioned is communications between Busovaca and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to Defence Exhibit 193, that is the one with the controverted date, 14 March or 14 April. Now, if you look at the third full paragraph, there's a reference there to an attack on Ahmici, the precise words being that "The BH army may attempt to launch an attack on Ahmici." Do you see what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, I see what you are asking me to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, at that date, the 14th of March, or even the 14th of April, would you say that Ahmici was a BiH controlled area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: On the 14th of April 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, would you say there's a difficulty in the idea of the BiH attacking a BiH held area?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this document speaks about the intentions of the army. It is an assessment by the assistant for military intelligence from the Busovaca Brigade. So, he is assessing along which axis the BiH army may be acting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: As a military man, would you say that it is more usual to speak of one military force attacking an area held by another military force?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Is it more customary for an army controlling a particular territory to attack another territory under the control of another army, or one of the armies? That is logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would you say that the effect of this warning that the BH army was likely to launch an attack on Ahmici should have put the HVO on guard as to possible developments in Ahmici, that because of this warning which the HVO received, the HVO should have been taking a particular interest in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in assessments which are made, this is the assessment of one brigade. So, similar such assessments probably came in from other brigades. So, then, all the assessments are given to the commander, or rather the Chief of Staff who forwards them on. What the commander would do upon receipt of that assessment is up to him to decide, whether he will use the units against which target, and along which axis. We were not those to judge about that, where the HVO units would be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Last document, 475E, I think. I think the Prosecution produced this. Am I right, Mr. Prosecutor, the Prosecution produced this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution produced this. Brigadier, do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes, the one, I recognise it from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, look at paragraph one. This is a BiH document, is it?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: On the 7th line of paragraph numbered one we see that the commander of the 303rd Brigade is being ordered to provide assistance to our forces in the village of Putis, Jelinak, Loncari Nadioci and Ahmici, he is being ordered to provide assistance. Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you say those words are different from words which direct the making of an attack on Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this order, as far as I can understand it, this commander order is issued once the units are already undertaking combat activities in those villages. And now this is simply stated as the assistance that has to be provided to them, as to which unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I return the matter to the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would just like to organise ourselves, first of all. I know that the interpreters have been working since 2 o'clock. I haven't got many questions to ask you, because many of the questions I wanted to ask were asked by my colleagues. I have two or three questions I would like to ask you, but before that, even though it's going to be short, I wonder whether the interpreters will agree with me. First of all, maybe we could finish with this witness and then maybe have a half an hour break, because this has been a very strenuous session, and then we will have the Status Conference. Do the interpreters agree with me? Yes? All do accept. In that case, you must be tired, Brigadier, but I have got a few questions to ask you. My first question is the one to which I authorise you not to answer; or even if you want to, you can confer with counsel for Mr. Blaskic, in case you don't want to answer. The documents, all the documents that you have brought to this Tribunal, is it the result of your personal sources only, or did the Ministry of Defence of Croatia give them to you? Please think over my question well. The reason why I would like to know is that I wondered maybe that you can consult the Defence counsel. I remind you, you are under oath, but maybe if you don't want to answer it, don't answer. In any case, the Judges will draw conclusions, whatever your answer is. My question, I repeat, is: Were these only your own notes, or did Croatia open its military archives to you? So, this is a very clear and personal answer, you can either not answer or consult with the Defence counsel; but in any case, I would like an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Defence counsel would like the witness to give an answer according to his personal conscience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Defence counsel. I understand. You can answer, but you are under oath, I remind you.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, all the documents which were at my disposal and which were presented here I have personally, with my notes and according to my recollections, that is the form in which I gave it to this Tribunal, that is, to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, the English answer is, the translation into English was, does not make too much sense. Maybe he can say how, who gave him the documents, and what were his personal notes. It was not clear in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What I understood was that all the documents that were brought by the witness was the result of his personal notes and his personal recollections. That is what I understood, and I did not want to ask any other questions of him about that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When we speak about documents, these are the orders. This is just one source, and his notes and his recollections represent another source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I did not mean the orders here. These are the documents of the Defence, I have not, I cannot interfere with. But what I meant were the maps and the schematics and so on. For all the rest is confidential between the witness and the Defence. My following question, which might probably be the last one, or the one before the last. When you worked with the intelligence service, did you have any political activities in the sense that you would give to your hierarchical superiors information about the atmosphere in the population, the general feeling, the context? Or else, you only satisfied yourself with military information?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Only the information, intelligence of military type.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. And when in the military hierarchy there were various, when various officers had some political positions that they expressed, were you aware of that, or not?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: During my work, and even today, I can say that I never engaged in any political activities, and I have been solely concentrating on my profession and on the job that I have been doing. I never had any impact or influence on the political activities. The tasks that I receive, I receive from my commander, and that concerns the military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe I can rephrase my question. During the weeks and the months before the attack on the 16th of April, did you have the feeling that in the HVO, which is a military organisation, so, it is something that you are familiar with, that the HVO could have a propaganda activity? Now we speak about your field of competence. Did you have the feeling that, in the months and weeks preceding the attack that is mentioned in this indictment, the HVO actively participated in a propaganda campaign against the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I don't know that it took part in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Taking into account your position, your job, your high responsibility and intelligence activities, you had no knowledge of some form of propaganda that could have been in the HVO, that the HVO could be distributing?

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: I cannot claim that it did not exist, that propaganda did not exist; but as a military man, I did not deal with such propaganda. My job was to gather information about the BH army in that time period, and also I had to make certain estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I will ask you the last question: From what you've said, I can draw a conclusion that in fact you wanted to tell us that there was some kind of a civil war between military forces, very organised military forces on both sides.

utterances.speaker: IVICA ZEKO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Brigadier, you have been very patient. You have been for quite a while with us, and thank you very much for your coming here to give us evidence. I would like to thank the interpreters, and now we are going to have a longer break, for half an hour, after that a Status Conference which will be in closed session, and that is why we are going to meet now at 16.30. And after that we will have a Status Conference which will be in closed session. 15 --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 3.54 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of September, 1998 at 10.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
